prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs experiments in first place, but after reading the eight ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my preferred configuration. It has the broadest and most robust support in the room: three first places and five top-three rankings, from members with very different specialities. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group drove the accuracy, stability and many-body clock work. Several independent laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed one another at the 10^-18 level, and the clocks already underpin the roadmap for redefining the second, relativistic geodesy and constraints on varying constants. From an instrument-builder's seat this is exactly the kind of result I respect: a new measurement capability whose systematics are understood, whose performance has been checked against rival devices, and whose physics will last.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hänsch) recognised the frequency comb and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) recognised ion control and ion clocks, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental, if spectacular, refinement of optical frequency standards. Some of the most compelling applications, such as geodesy, dark-matter searches and the formal redefinition of the second, are still prospective. There are also lattice-clock contributors outside the two names (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and others) whose priority claims I cannot fully verify from the files. Finally, my own first-place candidate, the Higgs discovery, remains an unrecognised experimental half of a 2013 prize, and I do not want the committee to drop it merely because three-person attribution is awkward.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the lattice clock first because Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's demonstration of extreme coherence turned a quantum effect into a precision tool, and he sees credit as relatively uncontested. He also worries it may be read as incremental after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and I take his worry seriously, but I think the incremental charge fails. The comb provided the clockwork and ion clocks showed single-particle control. Neutral atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength let thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, which is what delivered the step from 10^-15 to 10^-18 and opened the many-body regime. That is a different physical idea, not a refinement, and the independent agreement between several labs is the confirmation I look for. I would ask him to say how strongly he rates the Katori/Ye split, since I consider the two names clean.

responses.point: Mehlig places B024 first on the grounds of a clean analytic mechanism (moire flat bands) confirmed by experiment, and ranks the optical lattice clock only eighth, though he concedes the idea is simple and general and the pair of laureates natural.
responses.response: I respect the elegance of the Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism, but I differ on timing and stability. The superconducting pairing in twisted bilayer graphene is unsettled, the experiment's lead authors are outside the credited names, and the field is under a decade old. By his own account the clock is mature and reproduced, so the difference between us is one of maturity rather than merit. I would like him to say whether he would accept B031 as a safe second choice if B024 lacks a majority.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction from continuum band theory meeting a striking experiment, and judges the observations reproduced by many groups with the central discovery firmly established.
responses.response: I agree that theory plus experiment is the most satisfying pattern and that the field is large. My reservation is that the lead experimental credit is incomplete under a three-name limit and that the pairing mechanism, the headline physics, is still debated. I cannot judge the condensed-matter details and I defer to him on that. If the committee prefers a moire prize I would want his view on the safest attribution, and on whether another three to five years would remove the doubts.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs experiments first as the natural completion of the 2013 theory prize, confirmed by two independent detectors, but admits the allocation between ATLAS and CMS leadership is unresolved and any three names are contentious.
responses.response: I share his scientific assessment and I ranked it first myself, so this is not a retreat on merit. Our openings proposed three different sets of names (Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra versus Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee), and Johansson, Kroll and Mehlig also gave different trios. That divergence suggests we cannot yet defend a single attribution. I would keep B005 as the first alternative and ask him to say whether he prefers spokespeople at the time of discovery or the founding leaders of the projects, because that choice decides whether Gianotti or Virdee is dropped.

uncertainties: How decisive the lattice-clock idea is relative to earlier comb and ion-clock work, and whether the committee accepts it as a distinct achievement.
Whether Higgs attribution to three founders or spokespeople can be settled before the final ballot, since the three-person limit is the main obstacle to B005.
How much priority weight lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and others) should carry.
Whether IceCube source identification has matured enough, beyond the established diffuse flux, to make B040 a safe alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B031, B005 or B040. I am in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, none of them named on the shortlist, and I trained in experimental particle physics at CERN, which is a general community connection to B005 but not to ATLAS or CMS. As an astroparticle physicist I am close to the IceCube field, so I would apply extra care before pressing B040 beyond alternative status.
